_comment: Jargon tooltips for blog posts and project pages (beta-portfolio components/gloss-term.tsx). Keys are matched in post bodies: all-caps keys case-sensitively, others case-insensitively, first occurrence per page only. General technical definitions — nothing personal.
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — fetching relevant passages from a document store at query time and handing them to a language model as context, so its answer is grounded in those sources.
HNSW: Hierarchical Navigable Small World — a graph-based index for approximate nearest-neighbour search over vectors. A query hops through layered proximity graphs instead of comparing against every vector.
LLM: Large language model — a neural network trained on large amounts of text to predict the next token, used for generation, summarisation, classification and more.
noisy-OR: A way to combine independent signals into one probability: 1 − Π(1 − pᵢ). Each weak signal raises the total, without any single one having to be certain.
prompt injection: An attack where text reaching a language model — from a user, a document or a tool result — carries instructions that try to override the developer's intended ones.
guardrail: A safety layer around an LLM that checks inputs and/or outputs against policies, then blocks, rewrites or flags violations.
red-team: To attack your own system deliberately, the way an adversary would, to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
attack success rate: In red-teaming, the share of attack attempts that achieve their goal — e.g. the model actually complies with an injected instruction.
false-positive rate: The share of harmless inputs that get wrongly flagged — for a guardrail, the legitimate requests it blocks.
time-to-first-token: The delay between sending a request and receiving the first token of a streamed model response — what users feel as responsiveness.
spotlighting: A prompt-injection mitigation that marks untrusted text (e.g. fencing it in unique delimiters or encoding it) so the model can tell data apart from instructions.
sandwiching: A prompt-injection mitigation that restates the real instruction after any untrusted content, so the last word the model reads comes from the developer.
canary: A unique secret marker planted in a prompt or dataset. If it ever shows up in output, something has leaked.
taint: Taint tracking — labelling data by where it came from (trusted or untrusted) and carrying that label through processing, so untrusted data can be handled more cautiously.
PII: Personally identifiable information — data that can identify a person, such as a name, email address, phone number or ID number.
exfiltration: Getting data out of a system without authorisation — in LLM apps, e.g. tricking a model into embedding secrets in a URL or an image link.
structured output: Constraining a language model to answer in a machine-readable format, typically JSON that matches a given schema.
OpenAI-compatible: An API that accepts the same request and response format as OpenAI's, so existing clients and SDKs work with it by changing only the base URL.
ablation: An experiment that removes or disables one component at a time to measure how much each one contributes.
F1: The harmonic mean of precision and recall — a single score that is only high when a classifier both catches positives and avoids false alarms.
MCC: Matthews correlation coefficient — one score from −1 to 1 summarising a binary classifier's whole confusion matrix; robust when the classes are imbalanced.
ROC curve: Receiver operating characteristic curve — plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate as a decision threshold is swept from strict to lenient.
AUC: Area under the ROC curve — the probability that a classifier scores a random positive above a random negative. 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
embedding: A list of numbers (a vector) representing a piece of text, an image or audio so that similar meanings land close together — the basis of semantic search.
vector database: A database built to store embeddings and run fast similarity search over them, usually with an approximate nearest-neighbour index.
k-NN: k-nearest neighbours — finding the k items whose vectors are closest to a query vector under a distance measure such as cosine similarity.
pgvector: A PostgreSQL extension that adds a vector column type and similarity search, so embeddings can live alongside ordinary relational data.
multi-agent: A system in which several LLM-driven agents, each with its own role or tools, collaborate on a task and pass work between each other.
agentic: Describes AI systems that plan and take multi-step actions — calling tools, reading the results, deciding what to do next — rather than producing a single reply.
multimodal: Able to work with more than one kind of input — such as text plus images or audio — in the same model.
OCR: Optical character recognition — extracting machine-readable text from images or scanned documents.
CSP: Content Security Policy — an HTTP response header that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images and network connections a page may use.
JWT: JSON Web Token — a compact, signed token carrying claims (such as a user ID and an expiry time) that a server can verify without a session lookup.
OAuth: An authorisation framework that lets an app act on a user's account at another service through a scoped token, without ever seeing their password.
bcrypt: A deliberately slow, salted password-hashing function, designed to make brute-forcing stolen hashes expensive.
RLS: Row-level security — database policies that restrict which rows each user can read or write, enforced by the database itself.
WebRTC: Web Real-Time Communication — browser APIs and protocols for low-latency audio, video and data streams between peers.
HLS: HTTP Live Streaming — splits video into short segments listed in a playlist and serves them over plain HTTP. Plays almost everywhere, at the cost of several seconds of latency.
WHEP: WebRTC-HTTP Egress Protocol — a simple HTTP handshake a viewer uses to start playing a WebRTC stream from a media server.
RTSP: Real Time Streaming Protocol — a long-standing protocol for controlling media streams; the usual way IP cameras expose their video feed.
MediaMTX: An open-source media server that ingests live streams and re-publishes them over other protocols, such as RTSP in and WebRTC or HLS out.
ffmpeg: A command-line toolkit for recording, converting and streaming audio and video in almost any format.
WireGuard: A modern, lightweight VPN protocol with a small codebase and a fixed set of well-reviewed cryptographic primitives.
Tailscale: A mesh VPN built on WireGuard that links your devices into one private network, so they can reach each other without opening ports to the internet.
serverless: A hosting model where the platform runs your code on demand, per request, and manages servers and scaling for you; instances are short-lived and keep no local state.
cold start: The extra delay when a serverless platform has to boot a fresh instance to handle a request because no warm one was available.
rate limiter: A component that caps how many requests can be made in a time window — to protect an API, or to stay inside a provider's quota.
backoff: Waiting progressively longer between retries after failures — often exponentially, with random jitter — so a struggling service isn't hammered.
PgBouncer: A lightweight connection pooler for PostgreSQL that lets many clients share a few database connections. In transaction-pooling mode, session features such as prepared statements need care.
ORM: Object-relational mapper — a library that maps database tables to objects in code, so queries can be written in the programming language instead of raw SQL.
FTS5: SQLite's full-text search extension: it builds an inverted index over text columns so word and phrase queries run fast, with relevance ranking.
Storage Access Framework: Android's system API for opening, creating and browsing documents through a provider the user picks (local storage, cloud drives), with per-folder permission grants.
App Router: Next.js's routing system built on the app/ directory and React Server Components, with nested layouts and data fetching on the server.
monorepo: A single repository that holds several related apps or packages, sharing tooling and code.
PWA: Progressive Web App — a web app that can be installed and keep working offline, using a web app manifest and a service worker.
Manifest V3: The current Chrome extension platform: background pages are replaced by service workers, and remotely hosted code is not allowed.
glassmorphic: A UI style built from frosted, semi-transparent panels (background blur) layered over colourful backgrounds.
Minimax: A game-tree search for two-player games: assume the opponent always plays their best move, and pick the move whose worst case is best for you.
Alpha-Beta Pruning: An optimisation of minimax that skips branches which provably can't change the final decision — the same answer with far less searching.
U-Net: A convolutional neural network for image segmentation with an encoder–decoder shape and skip connections, producing a mask with a label for every pixel.
Attention Gates: Learned gates on a U-Net's skip connections that suppress irrelevant regions of the feature maps, helping the model focus on the target structure.
SHAP: SHapley Additive exPlanations — attributes a model's prediction to its input features using Shapley values from cooperative game theory.
BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training — a family of vision-language models used for tasks such as image captioning and visual question answering.
DSA: Data structures and algorithms — the core computer-science toolkit (arrays, trees, graphs, sorting, dynamic programming…) that technical interviews focus on.
